currentContext.business: TBO aggregates comprehensive travel inventory globally - hotels, airlines, cruises, car rentals, transfers, rail and insurance, sourced through direct APIs or supply aggregators - and distributes it to a diversified network of buyers: retail and API buyers such as travel agencies and independent travel advisors, and enterprise clients including tour operators, travel management companies, online travel platforms, super-apps and loyalty apps. Historically the industry focused on consumer-facing (B2C) channels while TBO targeted the underserved Business-to-Agent (B2A) pool, especially the premium and luxury segment, solving the complexity of a deeply fragmented global market. The Company describes itself at scale as 'an infrastructure layer that enables travel to be discovered, priced, booked, paid for, and serviced across geographies', with FY 2026 activity spanning air ticketing, hotels and packages, and a widening set of ancillary and connected-trip products.

The FY 2026 expansion programme has four strands. First, geographic and commercial reach: the Company proactively added local feet-on-street, built out sales and account-management teams, increased market-development effort and added servicing depth in priority geographies, entering 18 new countries with feet-on-street and increasing its source-market footprint by 6% to 150+ source markets and 6,000+ source cities; management is explicit that this expansion is not instantaneous, that hiring sales teams carries upfront cost, that newly onboarded agents take time to activate and mature, and that the full operating leverage from this investment cycle will therefore emerge only over time as cohorts become productive and the cost base stabilises. (PROVENANCE: this paragraph was routed to capex_expansion.txt under a '=== CHAIRMAN / MD MESSAGE ===' heading, not to this bundle.)|Fragmentation of high-yield demand structurally elevates the role of B2B travel intermediaries: success concentrates among global platforms able to aggregate highly fragmented supply, deliver unified multi-product discovery, provide rich content and execute cross-border fulfilment with robust post-booking support.|Three structural shifts management says are most relevant: travel is becoming more premium, experience-led and multi-product (raising the importance of connected journeys and curated supply); a meaningful portion of higher-value travel remains advisor-led and assisted; and AI is beginning to influence discovery, planning, servicing and workflow design.|Mix shift as the monetisation lever: Hotels and Ancillaries remained the largest and most profitable product, accounting for ~64% of consolidated GTV in FY 2026, benefiting from direct contracting, premium supply curation, strong international demand and cross-sell from air and other entry products.|Margin/cost narrative: commercial-expansion investments elevated SG&A growth in the first half of FY 2026; management states these expenses moderated from Q3 FY 2026 onwards and operating leverage started to kick in, and that prior to the March geopolitical disruptions gross profit growth outpaced cost growth. risks.risk: Geopolitical and regional disruption of travel corridors
risks.note: Conflicts, travel advisories, airspace restrictions, sanctions and aviation incidents may disrupt important travel corridors and affect demand patterns. This is not theoretical for TBO: FY 2026 saw an India-Pakistan flare-up, the broader Iran-US-Israel conflict, aviation disruptions, a major air tragedy and weather events, and March 2026 - a seasonally important period - affected both source and destination markets across approximately 40% of relevant travel corridors, producing weaker demand, cancellations and volatility in booking patterns. Airspace restrictions and instability in the Middle East are stated to have caused a 70% drop in demand in early 2026. Management's mitigation is geographic diversification across source markets, broader supply coverage, active corridor monitoring and reallocation toward alternate demand flows, and it explicitly concedes that diversification reduces exposure but does not eliminate volatility and that corridor risk remains real. Geopolitical Conflicts was newly ADDED as a BRSR material topic in FY 2025-26.

As a global B2B platform managing high-volume transactional, payment and customer data streams across multiple jurisdictions, the Company faces material operational and compliance exposure from systemic IT vulnerabilities; prolonged network outages, infrastructure failures or sophisticated cyber incidents can immediately disrupt downstream booking fulfilment, cause revenue leakage and severely compromise partner trust. Privacy and Data Security is the FIRST-listed BRSR material issue, rated both risk and opportunity, with the stated negative implication being exposure to legal penalties and significant breach-recovery costs. Mitigation is stated as enterprise-grade threat detection, data encryption, regular assessments, access controls, platform resilience, monitoring and audit, and strict compliance with applicable data-privacy regulations. The Corporate Governance Report separately makes cybersecurity and data protection a standing board-level oversight area.

risks.risk: AI-driven disintermediation of the distribution channel
risks.note: AI-enabled interfaces and agentic commerce models may increasingly influence how travel is discovered, planned, booked and fulfilled, creating intermediary bypass risk in simpler use cases. This is the risk most specific to the business model and management engages it directly rather than deflecting: its stated counter-thesis is that complex, premium and multi-component travel will continue to require expertise, robust fulfilment infrastructure, curated supply, servicing capability, payment infrastructure and operational reliability, and that AI bots will become demand channels FEEDING travel distribution platforms rather than replacing them. Mitigation is continued investment in AI-enabled workflows, infrastructure relevance, fulfilment capability and advisor-led complex travel. Note the two-sided nature: management also frames AI as a moat risk in the other direction, observing that frontier models can recreate an entire platform front-end at a fraction of cost and time, which is why it argues differentiation must sit in infrastructure, integrations, relationships and data systems rather than interface.

The business model depends on relationships with airlines, hotel chains, aggregators and ancillary providers, and changes in supplier economics, commission structures, pricing models or direct distribution strategies may affect profitability and competitiveness. The structural exposure is that suppliers can choose to go direct and bypass the distribution layer. Mitigation is expansion of direct contracting (direct supply share rose to 35% in FY 2026 from 33.9% in FY 2025), diversified supplier relationships and long-term partnership management.

risks.risk: Competitive intensity in global travel distribution
risks.note: The market remains highly competitive with global online travel companies, regional platforms, supplier-direct channels and specialist vertical players participating; competitive intensity may increase pressure on pricing, commissions, customer acquisition costs and margins. Mitigation is stated as continued investment in technology, servicing capability, supply breadth, premium travel positioning and differentiated partner workflows.

Inflation, interest rates, currency movements and slower discretionary spending may affect booking volumes, travel frequency, destination choices and traveller spend; currency weakness in outbound source markets may specifically affect affordability and mix. Travel is discretionary, so this risk is amplified relative to staples-like businesses. Mitigation is diversified market exposure, product mix toward higher-value categories, active commercial management and customer-cohort diversification.

risks.risk: Execution and cost-timing risk in the commercial investment cycle
risks.note: Not presented in the AR's risk table but flagged repeatedly by management as a live watch-item: hiring sales teams and adding feet-on-street carries upfront cost, newly onboarded agents take time to activate, mature and scale, and the full operating leverage from the FY 2026 investment cycle will emerge only over time as cohorts become more productive and the cost base stabilises. Management states these investments elevated SG&A growth in the first half of FY 2026 before moderating from Q3 FY 2026, and concedes that 'sales investments can create future growth, but they also carry upfront costs before operating leverage is fully visible' and that 'AI improves productivity, but it does not transform operating models overnight'.

risks.risk: Integration risk on the Classic Vacations acquisition and dependence on M&A for the North America build
risks.note: The North America strategy rests on a single acquisition. Management describes the integration - spanning platform, supply, commercial and talent - as an execution priority with expected completion by Q3 of the current fiscal (stated as FY 2027 in the Letter to Shareholders) and explicitly characterises it as 'a multi-year value creation journey' that is 'not complete'. The stated intent is not simply to consolidate Classic Vacations but to combine its advisor relationships, luxury supply and servicing expertise with TBO's technology, global supply network, commercial reach and operating discipline - a two-way integration that is correspondingly harder to execute.

A structural, quantified concentration risk that the AR discloses without labelling it a risk. BRSR Section A item 22 reports permanent-employee turnover of 30% in FY 2025-26 (male 28%, female 34%), 31% in FY 2024-25 and 32% in FY 2023-24 - a persistently high rate for a business whose moat is stated to rest on relationships, servicing capability and execution. BRSR also lists Employee Wellbeing and Employee Engagement and Development as material issues, noting that poor wellbeing results in higher attrition, reduced productivity and negative employer branding. The Company reports 2,600+ associates globally as of March 31, 2026 (1,543 employees on the standalone BRSR boundary) and states it strengthened its leadership bench with senior additions across people, supply and business leadership roles, with succession planning a standing board oversight area.

risks.risk: Product and geographic concentration on the standalone reporting entity
risks.note: A concentration disclosure that is a structural risk even though the AR does not label it one. BRSR Section A reports 100% of turnover from a single business activity - 'Travel Agency, Tour Operator & Other Reservation Service Activities' - with Air Ticketing alone at 49.85% of standalone turnover, Hotels & Packages 16.76% and Others 33.39%, and exports at 38.30% of total turnover. At group level the Airlines business is stated to be overwhelmingly India-weighted and to have been the segment most exposed to FY 2026's geopolitical disruptions, airspace interruptions and the airline crash. BRSR item 9 'Open-ness of business' also shows a very high related-party share of certain balances (sales to related parties 31.76% of total sales in FY 2025-26 against 26.76% prior year; loans and advances to related parties 85.17% against 5.76%; investments in related parties 98.30%) - expected in a holding-and-operating structure where the overseas business sits under Tek Travels DMCC, but a genuine intra-group dependency of the listed standalone entity.

thesis: TBO is a global B2B travel-distribution platform monetizing GTV via take-rate, with structural growth from (a) market-development investment (sales/KAM expansion → onboarding new travel agents and driving them through T1/T5/T10 transaction journey), (b) shift toward higher-take-rate markets (North America, Europe) and higher-margin hotels mix vs air, and (c) the luxury/curated adjacency (Classic Vacations + Voya AI tool). Q4FY26 demonstrated resilience: despite the war (started end-Feb) severely hitting its largest source market (Middle East) and Israel (a Top-7 source country), the company still grew YoY on both top and bottom line. Jan/Feb showed strong operating leverage and margin expansion; March was "a complete washout." Mgmt expects Q1FY27 better than both Q4 and the year-ago quarter, with green shoots of operating leverage as SG&A growth tapers below GTV growth.

themes.title: Hospitality & travel up-cycle
themes.need: Q1FY27 split hotels from airlines. INDHOTEL delivered a 17th consecutive record quarter - consolidated revenue INR 2,419cr (+15%), EBITDA INR 753cr at 31.1%, standalone occupancy jumping to 82% from 76% on a 41.8% standalone EBITDA margin, and asset-light management-fee income INR 168cr (+26%) - with management now framing the West-Asia war as a NET tailwind because outbound travel stays home; leisure RevPAR (Rajasthan/Goa) ran up high-20s. Airlines got the mirror image: INDIGO's EBITDAR margin collapsed from 28.0% to 15.6% on blended ATF of ~INR 140-150/litre versus INR 85-90 pre-war (fuel CASK +~80% YoY), leaving yield as the only defence. MHRIL shows domestic leisure premiumisation is real - Keystone average unit realisation +73% to INR 14.4 lakh on stable gross sales. LEMONTREE/CHALET/SAMHI/THELEELA ride the same occupancy-led room cycle; TRAVELFOOD/TBOTEK/DREAMFOLKS remain levered to airport PAX and B2B travel.
themes.driver: Occupancy-led (not rate-led) RevPAR compounding plus INDHOTEL's Ginger conversion cadence stepping 15->20->25->40 per quarter through FY27; for airlines the swing is INDIGO's guided Q2 PRASK growth of 'more than 25%' on flattish capacity against ATF cracks.

themes.title: Digital platforms, SaaS, payments & cybersecurity
themes.need: Digital-public-infrastructure scale, enterprise SaaS and a compliance/security upcycle drive a distinct platform cohort. PINELABS/NPST/CMSINFO on payments; AURIONPRO/NEWGEN/NUCLEUS/ROUTE/TANLA on banking/CPaaS software; EMUDHRA/META(544441)/AURIONPRO on digital-identity & cybersecurity; CAPILLARY/MAPMYINDIA/NAZARA on SaaS/geospatial/gaming. Q1FY27 anchored the payments leg: PAYTM's GMV grew 31% YoY (accelerating 23% -> 27% -> 31%) with merchant payments about 80% of the financial-services mix and 25-30 lakh device additions a year on a distribution-only lending model (no book, no FLDG); MOBIKWIK posted payments GMV of INR 52,400cr (+58% YoY), a 13th consecutive record quarter and India's largest wallet by GTV at ~20% share, against only ~INR 3,200cr of digital-credit GMV. one_liner.title: One Liner (RHP)
one_liner.body: TBO Tek is a global B2B (Business-to-Agent) travel distribution platform that aggregates fragmented worldwide travel supply and distributes it to retail and enterprise travel buyers through a unified technology, payments, credit and servicing layer.

business_model.title: What they do
business_model.body: TBO aggregates comprehensive travel inventory globally - hotels, airlines, cruises, car rentals, transfers, rail and insurance, sourced through direct APIs or supply aggregators - and distributes it to a diversified network of buyers: retail and API buyers such as travel agencies and independent travel advisors, and enterprise clients including tour operators, travel management companies, online travel platforms, super-apps and loyalty apps. Historically the industry focused on consumer-facing (B2C) channels while TBO targeted the underserved Business-to-Agent (B2A) pool, especially the premium and luxury segment, solving the complexity of a deeply fragmented global market. The Company describes itself at scale as 'an infrastructure layer that enables travel to be discovered, priced, booked, paid for, and serviced across geographies', with FY 2026 activity spanning air ticketing, hotels and packages, and a widening set of ancillary and connected-trip products.

guidance.body:

demand_drivers.title: Demand & outlook drivers
demand_drivers.body:
- Sector normalisation: FY 2026 is described as the formal stabilisation of the global travel sector, with international and domestic passenger volumes structurally returning to and surpassing 2019 baseline levels, and the operating environment transitioning from post-pandemic volatile demand spikes to a normalised, predictable growth trajectory with capacity stabilisation across commercial aviation and hospitality.
- Value-driven rather than volume-driven growth: management states the structural shift in gross booking value is increasingly driven by higher average daily rates (ADRs) and premiumisation rather than sheer volume expansion, with traveller spend allocating toward premium accommodation, longer stays and high-quality destinations.
- Global demand backdrop: international tourist arrivals reached approximately 1.52 Billion in calendar 2025, a 4% year-on-year expansion; Africa was the fastest-growing destination region by percentage growth, Europe maintained high volume baselines, Asia-Pacific continued a gradual multi-phase recovery, and the Middle East sustained volumes above pre-pandemic baselines.
- India as a structural demand pool: Indian national departures reached 32.8 Million in 2025, up 6.3% YoY and around 22% above the pre-pandemic 26.9 Million of 2019, with outbound travel growing at an estimated 15% CAGR since 2022; Domestic Tourist Visits reached approximately 4.28 Billion, around 45% YoY growth. Source stated as Ministry of Tourism, Government of India.
- India supply-side enablers cited as demand drivers: approximately 420 Million air passengers handled during FY 2026, an airport network expanded to 164 airports, over USD 170 Billion of aviation-infrastructure investment continuing through 2030, and 57 countries now offering visa-free or e-visa entry for Indian travellers. (PROVENANCE: this paragraph was routed to capex_expansion.txt under a '=== CHAIRMAN / MD MESSAGE ===' heading, not to this bundle.)
- Fragmentation of high-yield demand structurally elevates the role of B2B travel intermediaries: success concentrates among global platforms able to aggregate highly fragmented supply, deliver unified multi-product discovery, provide rich content and execute cross-border fulfilment with robust post-booking support.
- Three structural shifts management says are most relevant: travel is becoming more premium, experience-led and multi-product (raising the importance of connected journeys and curated supply); a meaningful portion of higher-value travel remains advisor-led and assisted; and AI is beginning to influence discovery, planning, servicing and workflow design.
- Mix shift as the monetisation lever: Hotels and Ancillaries remained the largest and most profitable product, accounting for ~64% of consolidated GTV in FY 2026, benefiting from direct contracting, premium supply curation, strong international demand and cross-sell from air and other entry products.
- Margin/cost narrative: commercial-expansion investments elevated SG&A growth in the first half of FY 2026; management states these expenses moderated from Q3 FY 2026 onwards and operating leverage started to kick in, and that prior to the March geopolitical disruptions gross profit growth outpaced cost growth. (PROVENANCE: Letter to Shareholders, routed to profile.txt.)
- Externalities as a persistent friction: airspace restrictions and regional instability in the Middle East led to a stated 70% drop in demand in early 2026; localised civil shutdowns, newly proposed tariff barriers and tightening cross-border compliance protocols escalate transaction friction and suppress inbound booking volumes.
- Management's stated AI view on demand: AI will reshape how travel is discovered and planned and will emerge as a powerful new demand channel, but fulfilment will still require global supply access, real-time pricing, payments and post-booking servicing - so travel distribution platforms remain critical infrastructure at the transaction layer and AI bots become demand channels feeding them.
- Outbound corridor evidence: hotel bookings grew by more than 20% across visa-friendly and short-haul destinations such as Vietnam, Bhutan, Seychelles, Kenya, the Philippines and Sri Lanka.
- Near-term recovery signal: elevated cancellations driven by the Middle East conflict are stated to be beginning to normalise, new sales across non-war-impacted corridors are steadily growing, and even directly impacted corridors are showing healthy underlying demand resilience. (PROVENANCE: Letter to Shareholders, routed to profile.txt.)

margins.body:

capex_expansion.title: Capex & expansion plans
capex_expansion.body: TBO Tek is an asset-light platform business with no manufacturing footprint - BRSR Section A item 18 states 0 plants nationally and 0 internationally, against 31 offices in India (0 international offices on the standalone reporting boundary) across 13 states - so 'expansion' in this annual report means commercial footprint, supply depth, product build-out and acquisitions rather than capacity. The FY 2026 expansion programme has four strands. First, geographic and commercial reach: the Company proactively added local feet-on-street, built out sales and account-management teams, increased market-development effort and added servicing depth in priority geographies, entering 18 new countries with feet-on-street and increasing its source-market footprint by 6% to 150+ source markets and 6,000+ source cities; management is explicit that this expansion is not instantaneous, that hiring sales teams carries upfront cost, that newly onboarded agents take time to activate and mature, and that the full operating leverage from this investment cycle will therefore emerge only over time as cohorts become productive and the cost base stabilises. Second, inorganic expansion: the acquisition of Classic Vacations in the United States (consolidated with effect from October 1, 2025) is the flagship project, described as acquiring a strategic enabler rather than GTV and as the platform to build North America at greater scale; a structured integration process spanning platform, supply, commercial and talent is underway with expected completion stated as 'by Q3 of current fiscal' in the Corporate Overview and as 'FY 2027' in the Letter to Shareholders, and the Company continues to look for larger, strategically aligned opportunities on top of the earlier Bookabed and Jumbonline deals. Third, supply and product build-out: expansion of direct contracting (direct supply share rose to 35% in FY 2026 from 33.9% in FY 2025), curated premium inventory through the Platinum programme, and new adjacent lines including ancillaries under the connected-trips vision, cruises, experiences, TBO Academy and the Voya itinerary and connected-journeys platform, whose early groundwork was completed during the year. Fourth, technology build-out: a dedicated AI Centre of Excellence was established as a structured multi-year adoption framework, and internally built platforms - Epicenter (in-house CRM and workflow platform, piloted and scaled for sales KAM in India) and Voya - are being positioned as long-term AI orchestration layers; roughly 75% of supplier-initiated tickets, 33% of customer-initiated tickets and 72% of system-generated tickets are now resolved through automated workflows. On the environmental side of capex, BRSR Principle 2 Essential Indicator 1 answers 'NA' for the percentage of R&D and capital expenditure invested in technologies improving environmental and social impacts, noting that the platform business is inherently low in energy intensity and that the Company leverages AWS auto-scaling so only required servers remain operational.

moat.title: Bull — competitive strengths
moat.body:
- Infrastructure-layer positioning: the platform brings a large and fragmented travel ecosystem together through a unified technology, payments, credit and servicing layer, enabling end-to-end cross-border discovery-to-fulfilment - a combination the Company argues is 'increasingly difficult to imitate'
- B2A focus on a structurally underserved pool: the industry historically chased B2C while TBO built for travel agents and advisors, especially in premium and luxury travel
- Two-sided network effects that compound with scale: over 55,000 unique agents transacted on the core TBO platform during FY 2026; the international transacting agent base grew 35% year-on-year; Monthly Active Agencies crossed 12,000 for the first time; around 8,900 new agencies transacted for the first time
- Direct supply depth: direct supply share increased to 35% in FY 2026 from 33.9% in FY 2025 (Directors' Report)
- Geographic diversification as a shock absorber: simultaneous market-share expansion across Europe, Asia-Pacific, the UK and Ireland, India and North America reduced structural concentration risk in any single corridor; management states this insulated aggregate booking volumes from localised disruptions
- Commercial-engine productivity: Key Account Manager productivity increased 43% year-on-year on a GTV basis (Directors' Report)
- Classic Vacations adds a hard-to-replicate US luxury franchise: 10,000+ annual transacting travel advisors, 1,500+ luxury hotel contracts, ~10 consortia with ~132K registered advisors and ~10K transacting advisors, a top-3 consortia relationship of 40+ years, direct connectivity with large chains including Marriott and IHG, average hotel booking value ~USD 8,600 and average daily room rate ~USD 1,000
- Validated inorganic-growth framework: the Bookabed, Jumbonline and Classic Vacations acquisitions are cited by management as validation of the M&A playbook
- Proprietary workflow assets: Epicenter (in-house CRM/workflow platform) and Voya (connected journeys platform), plus a dedicated AI Centre of Excellence, with roughly 75% of supplier-initiated tickets, 33% of customer-initiated tickets and 72% of system-generated tickets resolved through automated workflows
- Twenty-year operating history (FY 2026 report is the Twentieth Annual Report; incorporated 2006)
- External recognition for the acquired US business: Virtuoso 'Top Producing Tour Partner, Wholesaler USA 2026' and 'Highest Annual Growth award, Wholesaler USA 2026'; Travel Age West Wave Award 2026 'Best Packaged Tour Operator - Europe' and 'Favourite Packaged Tour Operator Representative'

risks.title: Risks
risks.body:
- Geopolitics/war: Middle East + Israel demand still below pre-war; recovery non-linear; further escalation a downside.
- Airline capacity cuts / fare volatility; corridor disruption.
- Working-capital/cash-flow drag if timing items don't reverse as expected.
- Global peers resetting take-rates lower → competitive pressure (mgmt comfortable).
- LATAM/Brazil structural FX + tax (IOF) headwinds.
- Classic integration execution (platform migration mid-way).

non_obvious.title: Non-obvious
non_obvious.body:

- Higher airfares are GTV-neutral-to-positive: fewer tickets for same GTV.
- B2B travel growing faster than B2C (online B2C saturating).
- Expedia's 20% B2B growth not viewed as direct competition (Expedia is also a TBO supplier).
- Classic carries negative working capital, but acquisition accounting subsumes opening benefit into investing CF — cash benefit only accrues as WC goes more negative going forward.
- AI: mgmt sees only internal productivity gains so far, no business-model disruption (MCPs/ChatGPT integrations not yet driving real business).
